nameStory: The Southern Moon Jelly gets its name from its translucent, moon-like bell that glows ethereally as it pulses through the water. The 'southern' part of its name reflects its preference for warmer waters compared to its close relative, the Common Moon Jelly. Like a ghostly full moon drifting through the ocean, this jellyfish creates an almost magical sight when spotted in New England waters.
description: The Southern Moon Jelly is a translucent, saucer-shaped jellyfish that drifts gracefully through coastal waters. Its bell-shaped body is nearly transparent with a subtle bluish or whitish tint, allowing you to see right through it like frosted glass. Four distinctive horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs are visible through the bell, appearing as darker patches arranged in a cross pattern. These jellies typically measure 6-10 inches across their bell, though some can grow larger in favorable conditions.

idTips.label: Four-leaf clover pattern
idTips.description: Look for four horseshoe or kidney-shaped structures visible through the transparent bell, arranged like a four-leaf clover - these are the reproductive organs that create the most distinctive identifying feature

idTips.label: Crystal-clear bell
idTips.description: The bell feels like firm jelly or thick plastic wrap when touched (though avoid contact), and is so transparent you can read through it like looking through a slightly frosted window

idTips.label: Gentle pulsing motion
idTips.description: Swims with rhythmic, umbrella-like contractions that create a hypnotic pulsing movement, much gentler and more graceful than the erratic swimming of other jellyfish

idTips.label: Short, frilly tentacles
idTips.description: Hundreds of very short, thread-like tentacles fringe the bell's edge, feeling slightly sticky if touched and creating a delicate, lace-like border

idTips.label: Mild sting sensation
idTips.description: If you accidentally touch one, you'll feel only a mild tingling or slight burning sensation, much less painful than a bee sting

habitat: Southern Moon Jellies appear in New England's warmer coastal waters, particularly in protected bays, harbors, and estuaries from late spring through early fall. They're most commonly spotted in shallow waters near docks, jetties, and calm beaches where the water temperature stays relatively warm. Look for them drifting near the surface on calm days in places like Narragansett Bay, Cape Cod's protected coves, and the warmer waters around Martha's Vineyard.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in late spring as water temperatures rise, though still uncommon. Early arrivals may be smaller and harder to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings in warm, calm waters. Most abundant during hot spells when they may appear in large groups called blooms.
seasonality.fall: Still present in early fall, especially during warm September days. Begin disappearing as water temperatures cool in October.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having moved to warmer southern regions or died off after reproducing.

funFact: Moon jellies are practically immortal in reverse - when conditions get tough, they can actually shrink themselves back into their juvenile polyp stage and start their life cycle over again, essentially hitting a biological reset button that lets them cheat death!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from Common Moon Jelly without genetic testing - both have the same four-leaf clover pattern and transparent bell. The main clue is location and timing: if you see moon jellies in New England's warmest waters during the hottest part of summer, there's a chance they're Southern Moon Jellies rather than the more common northern species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'southern,' these jellies do reach New England waters during warm periods, representing the northern edge of their range. The identification challenge between Aurelia species has only recently been resolved through genetic studies - what scientists once thought was a single worldwide species is actually many different regional species that look nearly identical.
compareHints: Southern Moon Jellies are virtually indistinguishable from Common Moon Jellies by appearance alone - both share the telltale four horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs and crystal-clear bell. The Greater Moon Jelly grows much larger and has a thicker, more robust bell, but is rarely seen in New England waters. Your best bet for identifying Southern Moon Jelly is finding them in the warmest available waters during peak summer heat.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Common Moon Jelly differs from its close relatives by its specific four-horseshoe pattern and North Atlantic location.
Greater Moon Jellies are typically larger than Common Moon Jellies, though their size ranges overlap significantly.
